Q7343.t: Turquoise lace stitched along Australia's coast
Q7343.s: Look for patches of turquoise and pale lace scattered over deep navy water, far off the Queensland coast. Each is a reef built by living coral, and together they form the largest coral reef system on Earth, running for about 2,300 km. It is so big that astronauts can pick it out from orbit.
Q7343.w: Turquoise and cream patches on dark blue sea, well offshore, lined up parallel to the Queensland coast.
f: It is made up of roughly 3,000 separate reefs and about 900 islands.
UNESCO listed the reef as a World Heritage site in 1981.
Once a year, a few nights after a full moon in October or November, its corals release their eggs almost all at once.

q.q: Roughly how long is the Great Barrier Reef?

Q118841.t: A mile-deep gash with Earth's history on its walls
Q118841.s: Even from 11 km up the Grand Canyon looks like a wound in the plateau: a jagged chasm of red, orange and cream layers, with the Colorado River a thin green-brown thread at the bottom. It is about 446 km long and up to 29 km wide. In places the river runs some 1,800 metres below the rim.
Q118841.w: A branching maze of red and cream cliffs cutting the flat plateau, the river hidden deep inside.
f: The oldest rocks at the bottom of the canyon are nearly two billion years old.
The North Rim is about 300 m higher than the South Rim, gets far more snow and closes to visitors in winter.
The Grand Canyon became a US national park in 1919.

q.q: Which river carved the Grand Canyon?

Q43278.t: A waterfall that announces itself with a cloud
Q43278.s: Before you see the falls you may see their cloud: a white plume of spray rising above the Zambezi, visible from dozens of kilometres away when the river is high. Below it the water drops into a narrow chasm about 1.7 km long, then zigzags through a chain of gorges. Locally it is called Mosi-oa-Tunya, 'the smoke that thunders'.
Q43278.w: A white mist above the Zambezi, then a sharp zigzag of gorges below it, on the Zambia–Zimbabwe border.
f: About 1,700 m wide and over 100 m high, it is one of the largest sheets of falling water in the world.
David Livingstone reached the falls in 1855 and named them after Queen Victoria.
The zigzag gorges downstream are former lips of the falls, left behind as the water cut its way back upstream.

q.q: What does the local name Mosi-oa-Tunya mean?

Q34221.t: Where Lake Erie spills over a cliff towards Ontario
Q34221.s: From the air, look for a white smudge of spray between Lake Erie and Lake Ontario: that is the Horseshoe Falls, curved just like its name. The Niagara River carries the outflow of four Great Lakes over the edge of the Niagara Escarpment here. The falls formed roughly 12,000 years ago, as the ice sheets melted back.
Q34221.w: A short river linking Lake Erie and Lake Ontario; the falls are a white patch where it bends.
f: There are three falls: the big Horseshoe Falls on the Canadian side, and the American and Bridal Veil Falls next door.
The falls are about 50 m high; creeping upstream, they have cut a gorge some 11 km long.
At night much of the river is diverted to hydroelectric plants, so less water goes over the falls.

q.q: Which two lakes does the Niagara River connect?

Q36332.t: Some 275 falls strung along one jungle cliff
Q36332.s: Iguaçu is not one waterfall but a whole horseshoe of them: around 275 separate cascades spread along nearly 3 km of cliff, on the border of Brazil and Argentina. From above, look for a brown river breaking into white foam inside green forest. The deepest point, the U-shaped Devil's Throat, swallows about half of the river's flow.
Q36332.w: White foam in green forest, just east of where the Iguaçu River meets the wide Paraná.
f: The river's name comes from the Guarani words for 'big water'.
Both the Argentine and the Brazilian national parks around the falls are UNESCO World Heritage sites.
Downstream the Iguaçu joins the Paraná at a point where Brazil, Argentina and Paraguay meet.

q.q: Which two countries share Iguaçu Falls?

Q3783.t: A café-au-lait river in an ocean of green
Q3783.s: Below you the Amazon, here still called the Solimões, is a broad café-au-lait band wandering through unbroken green, with side channels, islands and lakes along both banks. It carries about a fifth of all the river water that reaches the world's oceans. Not a single bridge crosses its main stream.
Q3783.w: A wide brown river with pale sandbars and dark lakes on either side, cutting through unbroken forest.
f: Its average flow is around 200,000 cubic metres per second, more than the next several largest rivers combined.
At Manaus the dark Rio Negro joins it, and the two waters run side by side for kilometres before mixing.
In 1500 Vicente Yáñez Pinzón found fresh water at sea off its mouth and named the river the 'Sweet Sea'.

q.q: What is the Amazon called in Brazil above Manaus?

Q3392.t: A green thread stitched through the Sahara
Q3392.s: Few sights from the air are as stark as this: a single blue-green line with a narrow fringe of fields and palms, and bare desert on both sides. Here in northern Sudan the Nile makes its Great Bend, flowing south-west for a few hundred kilometres before turning north again. Nubian kings built pyramids along this stretch.
Q3392.w: A thin dark line with a green fringe across pale desert, curving in a big S.
f: At about 6,650 km, the Nile is one of the two longest rivers on Earth, alongside the Amazon.
Sudan has more pyramids than Egypt, around two hundred of them, smaller and steeper than Giza's.
Its water comes from two sources: the White Nile from the lakes of East Africa and the Blue Nile from Ethiopia.

q.q: Where do the White Nile and the Blue Nile meet?

Q932289.t: Africa's great green heart, cut by brown rivers
Q932289.s: For hundreds of kilometres there is almost nothing but forest: a dense green carpet, cut by brown rivers that loop and braid through it. This is the heart of the Congo basin, home to the second-largest tropical rainforest on Earth after the Amazon. By afternoon towering thunderclouds often build over it, fed by moisture the trees themselves breathe out.
Q932289.w: Unbroken dark green forest with meandering brown rivers; in the afternoon, clusters of tall white storm clouds.
f: The Congo River crosses the equator twice as it curves round the basin.
Bonobos live only here, south of the Congo River.
In 2017 scientists mapped a huge peatland beneath its swamp forests, the largest tropical peatland known.

q.q: Which ape lives only south of the Congo River?

Q244451.t: The greatest river basin on Earth, roofed in forest
Q244451.s: Look down and count the shades of green: canopy, swamp forest, pale patches of grassland, and rivers the colour of tea or milky coffee. This is the Amazon lowland, where forest still runs to the horizon in most directions. In places, straight roads with side tracks cut into it in a fishbone pattern, the mark of clearing for farms.
Q244451.w: Endless forest crossed by winding rivers; near roads, rectangular clearings arranged like a fishbone.
f: The Amazon's drainage basin covers about 7 million km², the largest of any river on Earth.
Much of the rain here was first evaporated by the forest itself, recycled again and again as air moves west.
Dust blown across the Atlantic from the Sahara helps fertilise the forest's poor soils.

q.q: Where does much of the dust that fertilises the Amazon come from?

Q797.t: America's biggest state, and its emptiest
Q797.s: Below you is the Alaskan interior: dark spruce forest, a glitter of lakes and the wide braided channels of the Yukon and its tributaries, with hardly a road in sight. Alaska is more than twice the size of Texas. On a clear day the white bulk of Denali, North America's highest peak at 6,190 m, may stand out far to the south.
Q797.w: Dark forest, silvery lakes and braided rivers with almost no roads; snowy ranges on the southern horizon.
f: The United States bought Alaska from Russia in 1867 for 7.2 million dollars.
Alaska has a longer coastline than all the other US states combined.
In Fairbanks, in the interior, midsummer days last almost 22 hours.

q.q: From which country did the US buy Alaska in 1867?

Q5428.t: Taiga from horizon to horizon, for hours on end
Q5428.s: You can fly for hours over Siberia and see little but taiga: dark larch and pine forest, winding rivers and, in winter, snow that turns the whole land white and blue. Here, on the Central Siberian Plateau, the Lena, the Lower Tunguska and their tributaries cut deep valleys. Siberia covers roughly three-quarters of Russia.
Q5428.w: Endless dark forest and looping rivers in deep valleys; in winter, white snow with grey larch woods showing through.
f: Siberia covers about 13 million km², more than Canada or China.
Much of the taiga here is larch, which sheds its needles, so in winter the forest looks grey rather than green.
Lake Baikal, in southern Siberia, holds about a fifth of the world's unfrozen fresh surface water.

q.q: Which Siberian lake is the deepest on Earth?

Q866405.t: The bigger, older half of Antarctica's ice
Q866405.s: If you ever see this, it will be a white emptiness without edges: the East Antarctic ice sheet, more than 4 km thick in places and rising to over 4,000 m. Near here stands Russia's Vostok Station, where −89.2 °C was recorded in 1983, the lowest air temperature ever measured by a weather station.
Q866405.w: Flat white ice to every horizon, with no landmarks at all; blinding in the summer sun.
f: About 4 km beneath Vostok Station lies Lake Vostok, a body of liquid water sealed under the ice.
The East Antarctic ice sheet holds enough water to raise world sea level by more than 50 metres.
This ice sheet has been building up for more than 30 million years.

q.q: What lies about 4 km beneath Vostok Station?

Q530917.t: An ice sheet resting on a floor below the sea
Q530917.s: West Antarctica looks like its eastern twin from above, white, silent and endless, but beneath the ice it is very different. Much of its bedrock lies far below sea level, so the ice sheet rests in a deep basin that the ocean could reach. Scientists watch its glaciers closely, because they are among the fastest-changing on Earth.
Q530917.w: An unbroken white plain; towards the coast, dark mountain ridges and crevassed glaciers break through the ice.
f: Vinson Massif, Antarctica's highest peak at 4,892 m, rises in West Antarctica's Ellsworth Mountains.
If all its ice melted, world sea level would rise by several metres.
The Transantarctic Mountains separate it from East Antarctica.

q.q: What is Antarctica's highest peak?

Q76034.t: Billions of years old, and speckled with lakes
Q76034.s: From the air the Canadian Shield looks as if someone had shattered a mirror over the land: thousands of lakes of every shape, bare pink-grey rock and dark patches of spruce or open tundra, all scraped and polished by ice-age glaciers. This is the ancient core of North America. Some of its rocks formed when Earth was barely half a billion years old.
Q76034.w: A jigsaw of countless lakes and bare rock with streaks of forest; in winter, white lakes framed by dark trees.
f: The shield covers roughly half of Canada, wrapped around Hudson Bay like a horseshoe.
The Acasta Gneiss in the Northwest Territories, about 4 billion years old, is among the oldest known rocks on Earth.
Its rocks hold rich deposits of nickel, gold, copper and diamonds.

q.q: Which bay does the Canadian Shield wrap around?

Q147304.t: Land built grain by grain by the Yellow River
Q147304.s: Below spreads one of the flattest and most crowded farmlands on Earth: a fine mosaic of fields, villages scattered like grains of rice, and often a grey-brown haze over it all. Most of the plain was laid down as silt by the Yellow River, which has shifted its course across it many times. In June, ripe winter wheat turns it gold.
Q147304.w: A vast flat patchwork of small fields and villages, often under haze; green in spring, gold in early summer.
f: The Grand Canal, the longest artificial waterway in the world, crosses the plain between Beijing and Hangzhou.
In places the Yellow River flows higher than the fields around it, held between tall levees.
Around 1855 the Yellow River moved its mouth from south of the Shandong Peninsula to north of it.

q.q: Which river laid down most of the North China Plain?

Q602925.t: Grassland to every horizon, in the heart of Eurasia
Q602925.s: Here the land opens up completely: rolling grassland, green in May and straw-gold by midsummer, crossed by dirt tracks and dotted with salt lakes that flash white in the sun. The huge rectangular fields in the north date from the Soviet Virgin Lands campaign of the 1950s. In winter everything is white and scoured by wind.
Q602925.w: Flat to rolling tan grassland, straight dirt tracks, white salt pans and huge rectangular fields further north.
f: In the Virgin Lands campaign, begun in 1954, millions of hectares of Kazakh steppe were ploughed for wheat.
The lakes of Korgalzhyn, west of Astana, hold one of the world's most northerly flamingo colonies.
Saiga antelope, with their swollen, trunk-like noses, still roam the Kazakh steppe.

q.q: Which antelope with a trunk-like nose roams the Kazakh Steppe?

Q560549.t: Flat land from the North Sea all the way to the Urals
Q560549.s: You are over the north-eastern end of Europe's great lowland, which runs from the North Sea through Germany and Poland and across Russia to the Urals. Out here it is taiga and bog: dark forest, brown peatland glinting with pools, and rivers like the Pechora wandering in broad loops. In the west the same plain is a quilt of fields and towns.
Q560549.w: Dark taiga, brown bogs with glinting pools and looping rivers, stretching flat to the horizon.
f: On average the plain lies less than 200 m above sea level.
Its gentle hills and chains of lakes in Germany and Poland are moraines left by Ice Age glaciers.
The Pechora, which drains its north-eastern part, flows into the Barents Sea.

q.q: Which mountains mark the plain's eastern end?

Q12707.t: Where the land is ruled into squares a mile wide
Q12707.s: Look for the grid: roads a mile apart, square fields in green, gold and brown, and here and there perfect circles where pivot sprinklers water the crops. The Great Plains roll from Canada to Texas, east of the Rockies. Once shortgrass prairie grazed by tens of millions of bison, they are now one of the great grain belts of the world.
Q12707.w: A ruler-straight grid of roads and fields; to the west, the crumpled badlands of the Little Missouri River.
f: Much of the southern Plains is watered from the Ogallala Aquifer, one of the largest aquifers in the world.
The mile-square grid goes back to the Land Ordinance of 1785, which set out how US land was surveyed.
The Plains tilt gently east, losing well over a kilometre of height from the foot of the Rockies.

q.q: Why do many fields on the Great Plains look like perfect circles?

Q200952.t: A river that ties itself in loops
Q200952.s: Few rivers show their restlessness as plainly as the Ucayali. From above it is a brown ribbon coiling through the Peruvian rainforest, with a sandbar on every bend and abandoned loops lying beside it as crescent lakes. Its channel shifts year after year. Further north it meets the Marañón, and together they become the Amazon.
Q200952.w: Tight brown loops with pale sandbars and green crescent lakes beside them, in flat forest east of the Andes.
f: The Amazon's most distant source, high in the Andes of southern Peru, drains towards the sea through the Ucayali.
Pucallpa, the main city on its banks, is linked to Lima by a road across the Andes.
Riverboats run from Pucallpa down to Iquitos, a city with no road link to the rest of Peru.

q.q: Which river does the Ucayali meet to form the Amazon?

Q46841.t: A northern giant, braided around wooded islands
Q46841.s: Here, below Yakutsk, the Lena has already taken in the Aldan and the Vilyuy, and it spreads into a maze of channels and wooded islands, several kilometres from bank to bank. For about seven months a year it lies frozen, a white road through the taiga. In late May the ice breaks up with a roar and the spring flood covers the islands.
Q46841.w: A broad river split into channels around long wooded islands and sandbars; in winter, a white band through dark taiga.
f: The Lena is more than 4,000 km long and flows entirely within Russia.
In winter lorries drive for hundreds of kilometres along the frozen river on an ice road.
Upstream of Yakutsk stand the Lena Pillars, rock towers along the bank listed by UNESCO in 2012.

q.q: Into which sea does the Lena flow?

Q26076.t: Myanmar's great river, braided with sandbanks
Q26076.s: Through the dry heart of Myanmar the Irrawaddy is a wide sheet of brown water braided around pale sandbanks that grow and vanish with the seasons. Near here it takes in its biggest tributary, the Chindwin. A little downstream, on the east bank, lies the plain of Bagan, where more than two thousand old temples and pagodas still stand.
Q26076.w: A broad river with pale sandbanks in a dry, brownish plain; a second large river joins it from the north-west.
f: The Irrawaddy runs for more than 2,000 km, almost the whole length of Myanmar, to the Andaman Sea.
It gives its name to the Irrawaddy dolphin, a small, round-headed dolphin of rivers and coastal waters.
Its delta, laced with channels, is one of the great rice-growing regions of Asia.

q.q: Which old temple city lies on the Irrawaddy's east bank?

Q7821148.t: The Yangtze in its youth, on the roof of the world
Q7821148.s: Long before it becomes China's mightiest river, the Yangtze crosses the high Qinghai plateau as the Tongtian, 'the river that reaches to heaven'. From above it is a braided silver strand, spread in many channels over a broad gravel valley more than 4,000 m up. Around it lie brown-green pastures, snow-dusted hills and hardly any people.
Q7821148.w: A silvery river split into many channels across a wide gravel valley, among bare rounded hills of a high plateau.
f: In the classic novel 'Journey to the West', the monk Xuanzang crosses the Tongtian on the back of a giant turtle.
It lies in Sanjiangyuan, the 'Source of Three Rivers', where the Yangtze, the Yellow River and the Mekong all begin.
Below Yushu the Tongtian takes a new name: the Jinsha, the 'River of Golden Sand'.

q.q: The Tongtian is the upper course of which river?

Q1497.t: A river of islands between tall wooded bluffs
Q1497.s: Here, on its upper course, the Mississippi is not one channel but a whole valley of water: islands, sloughs and backwaters between steep wooded bluffs on both sides. The bluffs stand tall because this corner of the Midwest, the Driftless Area, escaped the last ice sheets. Every few dozen kilometres a lock and dam holds the river in a chain of broad pools.
Q1497.w: A wide valley of braided water and islands between steep forested bluffs, running north–south through farmland.
f: With the Missouri, the Mississippi drains about 40 percent of the contiguous United States.
Between Minneapolis and St. Louis, some 29 locks and dams turn the river into a navigable staircase.
Its source is Lake Itasca in Minnesota, where you can cross the young river on stepping stones.

q.q: In which state does the Mississippi begin?

Q1038418.t: The 'River of Golden Sand' in its deep valleys
Q1038418.s: Jinsha means 'golden sand', after the gold once panned from its gravels. This is the upper Yangtze, carving deep valleys through the mountains of Yunnan and Sichuan; from the air it is a green-brown thread at the bottom of steep, dry slopes. Today a chain of giant dams has turned long stretches of it into narrow, winding reservoirs.
Q1038418.w: A winding river deep in steep, brownish mountain valleys, widening in places into long, snake-like reservoirs.
f: Upstream, in Tiger Leaping Gorge, the mountainsides rise more than 3,000 m above the rushing water.
At the 'First Bend' near Shigu the river swings sharply from south to north-east.
The Baihetan Dam on the Jinsha is one of the most powerful hydroelectric plants in the world.

q.q: What does the name Jinsha mean?

Q4814791.t: A slow, pale river across the Sudanese plain
Q4814791.s: The White Nile is in no hurry. On these flat Sudanese plains it has almost no slope left, so it spreads wide and lazy between low banks, its water pale with fine clay, hence the name. Irrigated fields and reed beds line the river; beyond them, dry savanna runs to the horizon.
Q4814791.w: A broad, pale river with low banks and green irrigated strips, running north across a flat, dry plain.
f: At Khartoum it meets the Blue Nile, and for a while their different colours run side by side.
Its steady flow comes mostly from Lake Victoria and other East African lakes, filtered through the Sudd swamps.
The Jebel Aulia Dam, south of Khartoum, was built across the White Nile in the 1930s.

q.q: What gives the White Nile its name?

Q5413.t: Asia's longest river, held back by a giant dam
Q5413.s: Around here the Yangtze no longer flows freely: this is the Three Gorges reservoir, a green-brown lake some 600 km long, winding between steep hills. Towns that stood on its banks were rebuilt higher up the slopes as the water rose. Downstream, the reservoir ends at the Three Gorges Dam, the largest power station in the world by capacity.
Q5413.w: A long, winding, lake-like river between steep green hills, with towns climbing its slopes.
f: At about 6,300 km, the Yangtze is the longest river in Asia and the third longest in the world.
The reservoir behind the Three Gorges Dam reaches almost to Chongqing.
About a third of China's people live in the Yangtze basin.

q.q: Which dam holds back the Yangtze downstream of here?

Q2750140.t: The river that feeds Lake Victoria, and so the Nile
Q2750140.s: Look for a river winding through a wide valley of papyrus swamp, with lakes strung along it like beads. This is the Kagera, the largest river flowing into Lake Victoria, and its headwaters are often counted as the most distant source of the Nile. Along this stretch it forms Rwanda's eastern border, with Akagera National Park on its western bank.
Q2750140.w: A winding river in a broad green swamp with a chain of lakes beside it, among rolling savanna hills.
f: Its headwaters rise in Rwanda's Nyungwe forest and in the hills of Burundi.
Akagera National Park, named after the river, protects savanna, lakes and papyrus swamps along its banks.
The Kagera enters Lake Victoria in Tanzania, north of the town of Bukoba.

q.q: Which lake does the Kagera flow into?

Q5419.t: The 'Big Muddy', tamed into smooth curves
Q5419.s: The Missouri earned its nickname, the Big Muddy, from the silt it once carried. Here, along the Kansas–Missouri line, it swings in wide, smooth curves between levees, a channel shaped by engineers for barges. Look beside it for the ghosts of older courses: crescent lakes and curving field boundaries in the flat floodplain.
Q5419.w: A brown river in smooth, regular bends across a flat floodplain of fields, with crescent lakes and old channel scars.
f: At about 3,700 km, the Missouri is the longest river in the United States.
In 1804 Lewis and Clark set off up the Missouri on their expedition to the Pacific.
The Missouri joins the Mississippi just north of St. Louis.

q.q: What is the Missouri's nickname?

Q284780.t: China's lowest, hottest hollow, full of vineyards
Q284780.s: Look for a dark green oasis at the foot of red, furrowed hills, beside a white salt flat. This is the Turpan Depression, where the ground sinks to about 154 m below sea level at Lake Aydingkol, the lowest point in China. Its summers are the hottest in the country, yet Turpan's vineyards thrive on meltwater from the Tian Shan.
Q284780.w: A green oasis and a white salt flat in a brown desert basin, south of the snowy Tian Shan.
f: The Flaming Mountains, a bare red-sandstone ridge, run along its northern side and glow in the afternoon sun.
Karez, underground channels dug centuries ago, still carry mountain water to Turpan's fields.
Turpan is famous for grapes and raisins, dried in airy, open-walled brick houses.

q.q: About how far below sea level is the Turpan Depression's lowest point?

Q191333.t: A gateway through the mountains, used for millennia
Q191333.s: West of Peshawar the green, crowded plain ends abruptly against bare brown ridges, and a narrow valley winds up into them: the Khyber Pass. For thousands of years traders, pilgrims and armies came this way between Central Asia and the Indian subcontinent. Its highest point is only about 1,070 m, but the slopes around it are steep and dry.
Q191333.w: Where the green Peshawar plain meets a wall of bare, brown, folded hills to the west.
f: The Khyber is one of the main routes between Pakistan and Afghanistan, leading to the border crossing at Torkham.
A railway through the pass, with dozens of tunnels and bridges, was completed in the 1920s.
Gandhara, an ancient land of Buddhist art and learning, lay around Peshawar at the foot of the pass.

q.q: Which city lies at the eastern foot of the Khyber Pass?

Q118388.t: North America's lowest, hottest, driest valley
Q118388.s: Look for a long white streak between dark mountains: the salt pan of Badwater Basin, at 86 m below sea level the lowest point in North America. Fans of gravel spill from every canyon onto the valley floor like poured sand. In 1913 a thermometer here read 56.7 °C, the highest air temperature ever officially recorded on Earth.
Q118388.w: A long white salt flat between steep, bare brown ranges, with fan-shaped gravel slopes below each canyon.
f: Mount Whitney, the highest peak in the contiguous US at 4,421 m, stands less than 140 km away.
On Racetrack Playa, rocks slide across the mud when wind pushes thin sheets of ice, leaving long trails.
Death Valley is the largest national park in the contiguous United States.

q.q: How far below sea level is Badwater Basin?

Q534290.t: Australia's food bowl, threaded by slow brown rivers
Q534290.s: From above, the Murray–Darling basin is a vast, flat plain in ochre and khaki, crossed by slow rivers traced in the dark green of river red gums. In the Riverina, near here, irrigation turns the plain into bright green squares of rice, cotton and orchards. The basin covers about a seventh of Australia.
Q534290.w: A flat ochre plain crossed by winding rivers lined with dark green trees; bright green irrigated fields near them.
f: The Murray and the Darling together form Australia's longest river system, well over 3,000 km.
River red gums along its banks can live for several hundred years.
At dry Lake Mungo, in the west of the basin, people left traces of their lives more than 40,000 years ago.

q.q: Roughly what share of Australia does the Murray–Darling basin cover?

Q191566.t: Bog, taiga and gas flares on an endless flat
Q191566.s: Few places on Earth are as flat as this. Below you, rivers crawl across the West Siberian Plain in huge loops, and between them spread the bogs, a brown and olive patchwork of peat and countless small lakes. At night the gas flares and lights of the oil towns glow in the darkness.
Q191566.w: Flat olive-brown bogland spotted with small lakes, with looping rivers and dark ribbons of forest along them.
f: The Vasyugan Swamp, in the south of the plain, is one of the largest bogs in the world.
Across the plain the Ob drops only a few centimetres per kilometre, so its floods spread wide and linger.
The plain holds some of Russia's biggest oil and gas fields, among them Samotlor near Nizhnevartovsk.

q.q: Which huge bog lies in the south of the West Siberian Plain?

Q966943.t: A land of ridges where no river reaches the sea
Q966943.s: Look down on Nevada and you see a rhythm: a long dark mountain range, a flat pale valley, another range, another valley, repeating to the horizon, all running north–south. This is the Great Basin, where no river finds its way to the ocean; water ends in salt lakes or simply evaporates. Many valley floors are dry lake beds, dazzling white.
Q966943.w: Parallel north–south mountain ridges separated by flat, pale valleys, some with white dry lake beds.
f: Great Basin bristlecone pines, some almost 5,000 years old, are among the oldest living trees on Earth.
The Great Salt Lake in Utah is a remnant of a much larger Ice Age lake, Lake Bonneville.
Explorer John C. Frémont named the Great Basin in the 1840s, realising it had no outlet to the sea.

q.q: Where do the Great Basin's rivers end?

Q656985.t: A hidden sea of ancient water under the red outback
Q656985.s: Nothing on the surface gives it away: below you is the red and ochre outback, crossed by the braided dry channels of the Channel Country. But beneath it lies the Great Artesian Basin, one of the largest underground stores of fresh water on Earth. Some of its water fell as rain more than a million years ago.
Q656985.w: Rusty red plains laced with braided, mostly dry river channels that turn green after rare floods.
f: The basin lies beneath about a fifth of Australia.
Water from some deep bores comes out hot, close to boiling point.
Where the water seeps out naturally, mound springs form small green oases in the desert.

q.q: How old is some of the Great Artesian Basin's water?

Q28809720.t: Black-earth fields under a long white winter
Q28809720.s: The Manchurian Plain is northern China's great granary: a flat expanse of huge fields laid out in long strips, with poplar windbreaks drawn across them like pencil lines. Its soil is a rich black earth, darker than almost anywhere else in China. From November to March it lies frozen and white, then turns green with maize and soybeans.
Q28809720.w: Flat farmland in long strips divided by thin lines of trees; black in spring, green in summer, white in winter.
f: It is one of the world's few great black-soil regions, along with the Ukrainian steppe and the US Corn Belt.
The Songhua drains the plain north to the Amur, while the Liao flows south to the Bohai Sea.
Harbin, on its northern edge, is famous for its winter festival of giant ice sculptures.

q.q: Which crop, with maize, dominates the Manchurian Plain?

Q575516.t: Two deserts, two rivers and a vanishing sea
Q575516.s: Two green threads cross a sea of sand here: the Amu Darya and the Syr Darya, winding through the Kyzylkum and Karakum deserts of the Turan lowland. Along them spread irrigated fields and oasis towns. Both rivers once filled the Aral Sea, which has shrunk dramatically since the 1960s as their water was drawn off for cotton.
Q575516.w: Ochre desert with long dune ridges, crossed by green ribbons of irrigated land along two big rivers.
f: In Turkic languages Kyzylkum means 'red sand' and Karakum 'black sand'.
Khiva, whose walled inner town is a UNESCO site, stands in an oasis on the lower Amu Darya.
Much of the Aral Sea's exposed bed has become a new desert, the Aralkum.

q.q: What does 'Kyzylkum' mean?

Q23945221.t: The shore of the Sahara, green for only a few months
Q23945221.s: Sahel comes from the Arabic for 'shore': this is the coast of the Sahara, a belt of dry grass and thorny acacia running right across Africa from the Atlantic to the Red Sea. Its colours follow the rain. From July to September it turns green almost overnight; the rest of the year it fades to straw and dust, dotted with dark trees.
Q23945221.w: Tan or green savanna dotted with dark trees, fading into bare sand to the north, crossed by dry riverbeds.
f: The belt runs for roughly 5,000 km across Africa but is only a few hundred kilometres wide.
The Great Green Wall project aims to restore a band of land across the Sahel with trees and grasses.
Gum arabic, used in sweets and soft drinks, comes mostly from Sahel acacias, above all in Sudan.

q.q: What does the Arabic word 'sahel' mean?

Q756832.t: Flat pinewoods and farms between the hills and the sea
Q756832.s: Dark green pine forest, sandy fields in neat rectangles and slow rivers the colour of strong tea: this is the flat southern end of the Atlantic coastal plain. Once it was seabed, built of sand and clay laid down when the ocean reached further inland. Towards the coast it dissolves into salt marshes and a chain of barrier islands.
Q756832.w: Flat country of dark pinewoods and rectangular fields with winding tea-coloured rivers; marshes and islands near the coast.
f: Richmond, Raleigh, Columbia and Augusta grew on the Fall Line, where rivers tumble off the hills onto the plain.
The Okefenokee Swamp, on the Georgia–Florida border, is one of North America's largest blackwater swamps.
Georgia grows more peanuts than any other US state, much of them on this plain.

q.q: Why are many rivers here the colour of tea?

Q208347.t: A hot, thorny forest-plain at the heart of South America
Q208347.s: Olive-green felt, flat to every horizon: from above, the dry thorn forest of the Gran Chaco looks almost uniform. Look closer and you see the wandering scars of rivers such as the Pilcomayo and the Bermejo, and huge rectangular clearings for cattle and soybeans, edged with strips of trees left standing. The Chaco spreads across Argentina, Paraguay and Bolivia.
Q208347.w: Flat olive-green scrub forest with winding pale river scars and big rectangular clearings with tree-lined edges.
f: Its name is often traced to the Quechua 'chaku', a communal hunt or hunting ground.
It is the second-largest forest region in South America, after the Amazon.
The Chaco peccary was known only from fossils until living animals were identified here in the 1970s.

q.q: Which animal, once known only from fossils, was found alive in the Chaco?

Q141501.t: Plains that turn from dust to inland sea each year
Q141501.s: The Llanos swing between two faces. In the dry season, roughly December to April, this lowland along the Orinoco is golden grassland dotted with palms and crossed by dusty tracks. When the rains come, the rivers overflow and vast stretches become a shallow sheet of water shining in the sun. It is cowboy country, where llaneros still drive cattle across the plains.
Q141501.w: Flat grassland with lines of trees along winding rivers; in the rainy season, shining sheets of floodwater.
f: The Llanos stretch across Venezuela and Colombia, between the Andes and the Orinoco.
They are home to capybaras, the world's largest rodents, and to Orinoco crocodiles.
Joropo, the fast harp-and-maracas music of the llaneros, is Venezuela's national dance.

q.q: What are the cowboys of the Llanos called?

Q184382.t: Flat as a table, and ruled into giant fields
Q184382.s: Pampa comes from a Quechua word for a plain, and few plains are flatter. From above you see a quilt of enormous rectangular fields, dead-straight roads, shallow lakes shining silver and dark clumps of trees marking each estancia. Once tall grassland ridden by gauchos, it is now one of the world's great farm belts for soy, wheat, maize and beef.
Q184382.w: An immense flat quilt of rectangular fields, straight roads and silvery shallow lakes, with dark tree clumps around farmsteads.
f: Almost all the trees you see were planted: the natural pampas had grass but hardly any trees.
The deep, fertile soils of the Pampas are among the richest in the world.
Charles Darwin rode across the Pampas in the 1830s during the voyage of the Beagle.

q.q: What does the Quechua word 'pampa' mean?

Q192305.t: A plain of Himalayan mud, home to hundreds of millions
Q192305.s: Here the Ganges, now heading for the Bay of Bengal as the Padma, swings in wide braided loops across a plain so flat that its rivers wander at will. Every field, village and pond below you sits on mud carried down from the Himalayas. The Indo-Gangetic Plain is among the most densely populated places on Earth, and at night it glitters with countless lights.
Q192305.w: A wide braided river with pale sandbars in a flat green patchwork of fields, ponds and villages.
f: In places the river-laid sediments beneath the plain are more than a kilometre thick.
In winter a thick fog often settles over the plain, sometimes blanketing it from Pakistan to Bangladesh.
The plain runs for more than 2,500 km, from Pakistan across northern India to Bangladesh.

q.q: Which mountains supplied the mud that built this plain?

Q486324.t: A green oval oasis walled in by snowy mountains
Q486324.s: Look for a green oval set among mountains: the Fergana Valley, about 300 km long, ringed by the Tian Shan to the north and the Alay range to the south. Rivers pouring down from the snow feed a dense patchwork of cotton fields, orchards, mulberry trees and towns. The Syr Darya is born here, where the Naryn and the Kara Darya meet.
Q486324.w: A green, densely farmed basin surrounded on almost all sides by high, often snow-capped mountains.
f: The valley is shared by Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan.
More than 2,000 years ago Chinese emperors sought the famous 'heavenly horses' of Fergana.
Margilan, in the valley, has been known for its silk weaving for centuries.

q.q: Which river is born in the Fergana Valley?

Q51614.t: A high plateau of wheat, salt and ancient towns
Q51614.s: The heart of Anatolia is a high, open plateau about a kilometre above the sea, where wheat fields turn from green in spring to gold in summer and bare ochre by autumn. Just to the south-west lies Lake Tuz, a vast salt lake that dries into a blinding white crust in summer. Further south rise the cones of old volcanoes such as Hasan and Erciyes.
Q51614.w: A wide ochre and golden plateau; look for the huge white patch of Lake Tuz and distant volcanic cones.
f: The name comes from the Greek 'anatolē', meaning sunrise, and so the east.
Çatalhöyük, further south on the plateau, was a town of mud-brick houses more than 9,000 years ago.
Lake Tuz supplies a large share of Turkey's salt.

q.q: Which salt lake lies on the central Anatolian plateau?

Q1507.t: Wind, steppe and sky at the end of the Americas
Q1507.s: Patagonia from the air is mostly emptiness: grey-brown steppe and flat-topped mesetas, cut by a few river valleys that run like green threads from the Andes to the Atlantic. To the west the snowy Andes rise above deep blue lakes. The wind blows hard and almost constantly from the west, bending the few trees there are.
Q1507.w: Vast grey-brown steppe with flat mesas and canyons; to the west, snowy Andes and long blue lakes.
f: Welsh settlers reached the Chubut valley in 1865, and Welsh is still spoken in towns such as Gaiman.
Some of the largest known dinosaurs, including Argentinosaurus and Patagotitan, were found in Patagonia.
The name is usually linked to Magellan's crew, who in 1520 called the local people 'Patagones'.

q.q: Which European language is still spoken in Patagonia's Chubut valley?

Q605779.t: A vast slope of ice falling to the Southern Ocean
Q605779.s: From the coast of Wilkes Land the ice rises in a long, gentle slope towards the high plateau of East Antarctica, hundreds of kilometres inland. Near the sea, glaciers speed up and crack into crevasses, and their surface looks like crumpled paper. Beneath the ice lies the deep Aurora Subglacial Basin, much of it below sea level.
Q605779.w: A seamless white slope; near the coast, crevassed glaciers, ice cliffs and sea ice scattered on dark water.
f: It is named after Charles Wilkes, who charted this coast in 1840 on a US Navy expedition.
The Totten Glacier, on its coast, drains a large part of the ice sheet and is closely watched by scientists.
Australia's Casey Station stands on its coast, in the Windmill Islands.

q.q: Who is Wilkes Land named after?

Q1340442.t: Ice over some of the oldest rocks on Earth
Q1340442.s: Ice runs from horizon to horizon here, broken near the coast by dark ridges and nunataks, rocky peaks poking through the ice sheet like islands in a white sea. Some of those rocks are among the oldest on Earth. The coast was first sighted in 1831 by John Biscoe, a sealing and whaling captain sailing out of London.
Q1340442.w: A white ice sheet with dark rocky peaks near the coast poking through it like islands.
f: It takes its name from Enderby Brothers, the London whaling firm that sent Biscoe south.
Rocks of its Napier Complex are among the oldest in Antarctica, formed some 3.8 billion years ago.
Molodyozhnaya station, on its coast, was once the main Soviet base in Antarctica.

q.q: What kind of business gave Enderby Land its name?

Q189999.t: Mountains drowning in ice, named after a queen
Q189999.s: Near the coast of Queen Maud Land, jagged mountain chains break through the ice sheet, their dark peaks and granite spires half-buried in white. Further south, where you are now, the ice rises into the high polar plateau and the mountains vanish beneath it. The land's name honours Queen Maud of Norway, wife of King Haakon VII.
Q189999.w: A white plateau inland; towards the coast, dark mountain ranges and needle-like peaks sticking out of the ice.
f: It stretches for more than 2,000 km along the Antarctic coast.
Several countries run research stations here, among them Norway's Troll, Germany's Neumayer and India's Maitri.
Queen Maud was born a British princess, a daughter of King Edward VII.

q.q: Queen Maud, who gave this land its name, was queen of which country?

Q745767.t: Volcanoes under ice, named after an explorer's wife
Q745767.s: Here and there the ice of Marie Byrd Land is pierced by the snowy cones of volcanoes, some rising more than 4 km high. Mount Sidley, about 4,285 m, is the highest volcano in Antarctica. Around them lie hundreds of kilometres of flat white ice. The American aviator Richard Byrd named this remote corner of West Antarctica after his wife, Marie, in 1929.
Q745767.w: A white expanse with isolated, broad volcanic cones rising above the ice towards the coast.
f: No country has ever made a territorial claim to Marie Byrd Land.
In 1929 Byrd was among the first to fly over the South Pole.
Its coast faces the Amundsen and Ross seas, often choked with sea ice.

q.q: Who was Marie Byrd Land named after?

Q80299.t: The world's highest waterfall, off a table mountain
Q80299.s: Angel Falls drops 979 m from the edge of Auyán-tepui, a flat-topped sandstone mountain rising sheer out of the Venezuelan rainforest. It is the highest uninterrupted waterfall in the world; in the dry season much of the water turns to mist before it reaches the bottom. Look for dark tabletop mountains with vertical walls, often wrapped in cloud.
Q80299.w: Dark, flat-topped mountains with sheer cliff walls rising from green forest, often half-hidden in cloud.
f: It is named after Jimmie Angel, an American pilot who flew over it in 1933 and landed on the tepui in 1937.
In the local Pemón language it is called Kerepakupai Merú.
The falls lie in Canaima National Park, a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1994.

q.q: How high is Angel Falls?

Q599529.t: The steppe where the horse was probably first tamed
Q599529.s: From the Danube to the Urals, the Pontic-Caspian steppe was once a sea of feather grass. Today, near the Volga, it is mostly ploughed into vast fields of black earth, crossed by shelter belts of trees and cut by branching ravines. In early summer the wheat is green; by August the whole land turns gold and dusty.
Q599529.w: Huge fields in green, gold or black, divided by thin lines of trees and cut by branching ravines; the Volga to the west.
f: A genetic study published in 2021 traced modern domestic horses to this steppe, some 4,200 years ago.
Its black soils, chernozems, are among the most fertile on Earth.
For thousands of years nomads such as the Scythians and Sarmatians roamed this grassland.

q.q: Which animal was probably first domesticated on this steppe?

ne-rg-1730073989.t: The Corn Belt's heartland, ironed flat by glaciers
ne-rg-1730073989.s: A checkerboard to the horizon: this is the heart of America's Corn Belt, land flattened and enriched by ice-age glaciers and wind-blown dust, then ruled into square-mile sections. In summer the squares are green with maize and soybeans; after harvest they turn brown and tan. Rivers such as the Mississippi wind through it in wooded valleys.
ne-rg-1730073989.w: A square-mile grid of fields and roads, green in summer and brown after harvest, cut by wooded river valleys.
f: Iowa and Illinois, both in the Central Lowland, together grow roughly a third of the US maize crop.
Much of the soil formed on loess, fine dust blown off glacial outwash at the end of the Ice Age.
Before farming, most of this land was tallgrass prairie, with grasses taller than a person.

q.q: Which two crops fill the Corn Belt's summer checkerboard?

Q2016601.t: The 'Big Land' tundra of lakes and reindeer
Q2016601.s: East of the Pechora River spreads the Bolshezemelskaya Tundra, the 'Big Land' tundra: a treeless plain of moss, dwarf birch and low hills, glittering with thousands of lakes. For most of the year it is white; in summer it turns green and brown, and the lakes shine like scattered mirrors. Nenets herders still move their reindeer across it with the seasons.
Q2016601.w: A flat, treeless plain spattered with countless lakes and low rounded hills; white for most of the year.
f: Permafrost lies beneath the tundra, which is why meltwater gathers in so many shallow lakes.
Vorkuta, a coal-mining city, stands on its south-eastern edge.
Its name sets it against the smaller Malozemelskaya, or 'Small Land', Tundra west of the Pechora.

q.q: Which people herd reindeer on the Bolshezemelskaya Tundra?

Q252609.t: A slice of Antarctica first mapped from the air
Q252609.s: In 1938–39 a German expedition catapulted seaplanes off the ship Schwabenland and photographed this stretch of Queen Maud Land from the air, naming it New Swabia after the ship. Behind the flat coastal ice shelves the land climbs into dark mountain ranges, then vanishes under the polar plateau. Near the coast lies the Schirmacher Oasis, a rare strip of bare rock and lakes.
Q252609.w: Flat ice shelves at the coast, then dark mountain chains poking through the ice, and white plateau beyond.
f: The Schirmacher Oasis, about 17 km long, holds dozens of lakes and two stations, Russia's Novolazarevskaya and India's Maitri.
The ship Schwabenland was named after Swabia, a region of south-western Germany.
Novolazarevskaya honours Mikhail Lazarev, who sailed with Bellingshausen when Antarctica was sighted in 1820.

q.q: What gave New Swabia its name?

Q973.t: A wandering giant across the Siberian bogs
Q973.s: The Ob does not so much flow as wander: here, in the middle of the West Siberian Plain, it spreads into a broad floodplain of channels, oxbow lakes and willow-covered islands, in places tens of kilometres wide. In May and June the spring flood turns much of it into one shining sheet. Then the water slowly retreats to the main channel.
Q973.w: A broad silvery floodplain with many channels, oxbow lakes and islands, winding through flat bog and taiga.
f: With the Irtysh, the Ob forms one of Asia's longest river systems, about 5,400 km.
It ends in the Gulf of Ob, an estuary some 800 km long opening onto the Kara Sea.
The river lies under ice for around half the year.

q.q: Into which sea does the Gulf of Ob open?

Q1538813.t: The first thread of the Yangtze, below the glaciers
Q1538813.s: This braided stream, shining in a wide stony valley more than 4,500 m up, is the Tuotuo, the headwater usually counted as the official source of the Yangtze. It is born in the glaciers of Geladaindong in the Tanggula Mountains. Near the tiny settlement of Tuotuohe, the Qinghai–Tibet railway and highway cross it on long bridges.
Q1538813.w: A thin, braided silver stream spread across a broad grey-brown valley, with snowy peaks to the south-west.
f: Geladaindong, the peak whose glaciers feed the Tuotuo, rises to about 6,600 m.
Winters here are long and bitter, and the river freezes for several months each year.
Some surveys find the Dangqu, another headstream, to be longer, so the Yangtze's true source is still debated.

q.q: Which great river begins with the Tuotuo?

ne-rv-1159113693.t: The Nile's western arm, and the stone that spoke
ne-rv-1159113693.s: Below Cairo the Nile splits in two, and this is its western arm, the Rosetta Branch, winding north through the delta to the Mediterranean. From above it is a dark thread through a dense green quilt of fields and villages, sharply edged by desert to the west. Near its mouth, at Rosetta, French soldiers found the Rosetta Stone in 1799.
ne-rv-1159113693.w: A winding dark river through a dense green delta of fields and villages, with desert close by to the west.
f: The Rosetta Stone bears one decree in hieroglyphs, demotic and Greek, which helped scholars decipher hieroglyphs.
The town at its mouth is called Rashid in Arabic; Rosetta is its European name.
With the Damietta Branch, it frames the Nile Delta, one of the oldest farmed landscapes on Earth.

q.q: What famous object was found near the mouth of the Rosetta Branch?

ne-rv-1159113949.t: The Nile's eastern arm through a crowded green delta
ne-rv-1159113949.s: Where the Nile fans out into its delta, the Damietta Branch takes the eastern route to the sea. From the air it is a dark, gently winding line through an intensely green and crowded land, where fields, canals and villages leave hardly a gap. At night the whole delta sparkles with lights, framed by the black of the desert.
ne-rv-1159113949.w: A dark winding river through an intensely green, crowded delta; at night, a web of lights edged by dark desert.
f: The city of Mansoura stands on its banks, and Damietta lies near its mouth on the Mediterranean.
Damietta has long been Egypt's great centre of furniture-making.
Since the Aswan High Dam, the Nile's floods no longer reach the delta, and in places its coast is retreating.

q.q: Which of the Nile's two delta branches is the eastern one?

Q1653.t: Europe's great river squeezed through the Iron Gates
Q1653.s: Here the Danube forces its way through the Carpathians in the Iron Gates, a chain of gorges on the border of Serbia and Romania. From above the wide river suddenly narrows between steep wooded cliffs, then broadens again into a long reservoir behind the Iron Gate dam. At its narrowest, in the Kazan gorge, it is only about 150 m wide.
Q1653.w: A broad river pinched between steep forested mountains into a narrow, winding gorge, with a large dam downstream.
f: The Danube flows through or along ten countries, more than any other river in the world.
On a cliff near Orșova, the face of the Dacian king Decebalus is carved about 55 m high.
The river runs some 2,850 km, from Germany's Black Forest to the Black Sea.

q.q: How many countries does the Danube flow through or along?

Q26301.t: The far-flung Mongolian source of the Yenisey
Q26301.s: The Ider starts high in the Khangai Mountains of Mongolia and winds north-east through treeless steppe and valleys dotted with larch. From above it looks modest, a blue-grey thread with a thin green edge, but it is the most distant headstream of an enormous system: through the Selenga, Lake Baikal, the Angara and the Yenisey, its water reaches the Arctic Ocean.
Q26301.w: A thin winding river with a narrow green fringe in a broad valley of brownish steppe, dark larch on north slopes.
f: Where the Ider meets the Delgermörön, the Selenga River begins.
Measured from the Ider's source, the Yenisey is one of the world's longest river systems, over 5,000 km.
The river lies frozen for about half the year.

q.q: Which lake does the Ider's water pass through on its way to the Arctic?

Q75745.t: The river that fills Lake Baikal
Q75745.s: The Selenga gathers the rivers of northern Mongolia and carries them north into Russia and on to Lake Baikal. Here, near the border, it winds through a broad valley between steppe and pine-clad hills, splitting around islands and gravel bars. It brings in about half of all the water that flows into Baikal.
Q75745.w: A winding river with islands and gravel bars in a wide valley between steppe and dark pine-covered hills.
f: Where it enters Baikal, the Selenga has built a large delta, a maze of channels, reeds and lakes.
It is the largest river in Mongolia by volume of water.
Ulan-Ude, the capital of Buryatia, stands on the Selenga.

q.q: About how much of Lake Baikal's inflow comes from the Selenga?

Q15954437.t: The Brahmaputra's first steps, at the 'Horse Spring'
Q15954437.s: Far out in western Tibet, a young river wanders over a wide, windswept valley more than 4,500 m up, braided into silver channels between sand and gravel. This is the Maquan, the uppermost course of the Yarlung Tsangpo, which later becomes the Brahmaputra. Its source lies in glaciers south-east of sacred Mount Kailash and Lake Manasarovar.
Q15954437.w: A braided silver river spread over a broad, dry, sandy valley, with snowy Himalayan peaks to the south.
f: Maquan means 'Horse Spring', echoing its Tibetan name Tamchok Khabab, 'from the horse's mouth'.
In Tibetan tradition four great rivers rise near Kailash, from the mouths of a horse, a lion, an elephant and a peacock.
Below the town of Saga the river takes the name Yarlung Tsangpo.

q.q: Which great river begins as the Maquan?

Q162737.t: The only river that escapes from Lake Baikal
Q162737.s: More than 300 rivers flow into Lake Baikal, but only one flows out: the Angara. Here, far downstream, it crosses dark taiga as a broad, lake-like reservoir, one step in a staircase of dams that turn its fall into power. Its water is famously clear, and below the dams it often steams in winter instead of freezing.
Q162737.w: A broad, lake-like reservoir with branching bays in dark taiga, narrowing to a river below the dams.
f: The Angara is the largest tributary of the Yenisey, which it joins far to the west.
The Bratsk reservoir on the Angara is one of the largest artificial lakes in the world by volume.
A Buryat legend tells how Angara, Baikal's daughter, ran away to her beloved, the Yenisey.

q.q: How many rivers flow out of Lake Baikal?

Q2220.t: A deep green valley through Canada's northern farmland
Q2220.s: Look for a surprisingly deep valley cut into flat farmland: the Peace River, winding in broad curves some 200 m below the prairie, its slopes dark with aspen and spruce. Around it lies the Peace Country, some of the northernmost farmland in North America, gold with grain in late summer. Downstream the river swings north towards Lake Athabasca and the Arctic.
Q2220.w: A deep, winding, forested valley slicing through flat patchwork farmland of gold and green fields.
f: Its name recalls a peace made in the 18th century between the Cree and the Dane-zaa, or Beaver, people.
Near Lake Athabasca it feeds the Peace–Athabasca Delta, one of the largest inland freshwater deltas on Earth.
In British Columbia the W. A. C. Bennett Dam holds its water in Williston Lake, the province's largest lake.

q.q: Where does the Peace River's name come from?

Q3411.t: Canada's longest river, on its way to the Arctic
Q3411.s: The Mackenzie flows north for more than 1,700 km from Great Slave Lake to the Beaufort Sea, and here it is a wide, grey-brown river between dark spruce forest and the ridges of the Franklin Mountains. Nearby the clear Great Bear River flows into it. In winter the Mackenzie freezes hard and becomes an ice road linking remote communities.
Q3411.w: A broad, muddy river winding north through dark spruce forest, with low mountain ridges along its eastern side.
f: With its headwaters, the Mackenzie system runs about 4,200 km, the second longest in North America.
Its Dene name, Deh Cho, means 'big river'.
It is named after Alexander Mackenzie, who travelled down it to the Arctic Ocean in 1789.

q.q: Which lake does the Mackenzie flow out of?

ne-rv-1159117999.t: The Mekong as a mountain stream on the Tibetan Plateau
ne-rv-1159117999.s: It is hard to believe that this stream, winding through high grassland and rocky gorges in Qinghai, will one day become the mighty Mekong. The Za Qu, as the upper Mekong is called here, flows more than 4,000 m above the sea, past yak pastures and steep valley walls. It rises in small glaciers on the plateau and runs south-east towards Tibet.
ne-rv-1159117999.w: A winding river in a deep, narrow valley cut into high, bare grassland hills, often dusted with snow.
f: At Qamdo in Tibet it joins the Ang Qu, and from there it is called the Lancang, China's name for the Mekong.
The Mekong then flows through six countries on its way to the South China Sea.
Its source, above 5,000 m, lies in Zadoi County, within the Sanjiangyuan 'Source of Three Rivers' area.

q.q: The Za Qu is the upper course of which river?

Q21847787.t: South America's second great river, laced with islands
Q21847787.s: After the Amazon, the Paraná is South America's mightiest river, draining a huge basin across Brazil, Paraguay and Argentina together with its great tributary, the Paraguay. From above it is a broad brown band split by islands and sandbars, with floodplain lakes and marshes glinting on either side. It ends in a vast delta near Buenos Aires, feeding the Río de la Plata.
Q21847787.w: A broad brown river laced with islands and sandbars, with lagoons and marshes spreading across its floodplain.
f: At about 4,900 km, it is the second-longest river in South America.
The Itaipu Dam on the Paraná, between Brazil and Paraguay, is one of the world's largest hydroelectric plants.
The Paraná Delta, just north of Buenos Aires, is a maze of islands and channels where houses stand on stilts.

q.q: Which estuary does the Paraná flow into?

Q836812.t: The upper Congo, once thought to be the Nile
Q836812.s: The Lualaba is the Congo River in its youth, rising on the Katanga plateau and flowing north through savanna, gorges and a chain of marshy lakes. From the air it is a dark ribbon edged with swamp and pale floodplain grass. In the 1870s explorers still argued whether it fed the Nile or the Congo; Henry Morton Stanley settled it by following it to the Atlantic.
Q836812.w: A dark winding river edged by swamps and pale floodplains, with lakes strung along it, in green-brown savanna.
f: David Livingstone believed the Lualaba might be the upper Nile.
At Boyoma Falls, near Kisangani, the Lualaba ends and the river is called the Congo.
Upemba National Park, along its upper course, protects a chain of lakes and wetlands.

q.q: Which explorer followed the Lualaba all the way to the Atlantic?

Q2226.t: A short, wide river where pelicans nest on the rapids
Q2226.s: The Slave River carries the water of the Peace River and Lake Athabasca north to Great Slave Lake, a wide brown river winding through spruce forest and wetlands. Near Fort Smith it tumbles over a series of rapids, the main barrier on the long waterway from Alberta to the Arctic. On rocky islands in those rapids, American white pelicans nest.
Q2226.w: A broad, muddy river meandering through green forest and wetland, with white rapids near the Alberta border.
f: The pelicans at Fort Smith form the most northerly breeding colony of American white pelicans.
The river takes its name from 'Slavey', an old name for the Dene people living along it.
It flows along the edge of Wood Buffalo National Park, the largest national park in Canada.

q.q: Which bird nests on islands in the Slave River rapids?

Q41179.t: Six countries, one river, starting in Yunnan's gorges
Q41179.s: In Yunnan the Mekong, known in China as the Lancang, runs south through deep, forested valleys, much of it now stepped into long, narrow reservoirs behind a chain of dams. From above it looks like a green-brown snake coiled between steep ridges. From here it still has thousands of kilometres to go, past Laos, Thailand, Cambodia and Vietnam to its delta.
Q41179.w: A long, narrow, winding river or reservoir deep between steep green ridges, running roughly north–south.
f: The Mekong runs for more than 4,000 km, through or along six countries.
Its river fisheries are among the largest in the world and feed millions of people.
Each rainy season the Mekong's flood pushes water backwards up the Tonlé Sap river into Cambodia's great lake.

q.q: What is the Mekong called in China?

Q2599627.t: A great river flowing more than 3.5 km above the sea
Q2599627.s: If you are landing at Lhasa, this is the river beside the runway: the Yarlung Tsangpo, braided across a broad valley floor some 3,600 m up, with golden sand dunes piled against the slopes. It flows east along the Himalayas, then bursts through them in one of the deepest canyons on Earth and becomes the Brahmaputra in India.
Q2599627.w: A wide, braided river with pale sandbars and dunes in a broad valley between bare brown mountains.
f: Its Great Canyon, around the peak Namcha Barwa, is often called the deepest in the world.
Much of its Tibetan course lies above 3,000 m, making it one of the highest major rivers on Earth.
The Lhasa River, which flows past the Tibetan capital, joins it just west of here.
